In the anime, the story spends very little time on Violet's origins. The anime does a lot of showing and little telling, so when I watched it, I noticed:

1) Violet has considerable instincts and skills for combat, self-defense, threat detection, etc.

2) Violet has no apparent memories of parents, teachers, culture, family, race, nation, etc.

3) Violet was considered sexy as soon as human men saw her. They tried to rape her and she instantly, effortlessly killed them.

4) Violet is not just an innocent virgin, she is a total blank slate.

The anime did not explain much, but I thought that I had enough information to make a reasonable guess. Clearly, Violet had been taught to fight without any kind of human teacher. Thus the fighting knowledge must have been uploaded; thus she must be some kind of replicant. It seemed clear to me that some war-oriented laboratory had been making artificial humans for use as soldiers, and programmed these artificial humans with super-science. Thus the replicants had innate fighting skills but no memories of being taught to fight, no memories of sparring partners, etc.

And then the guy who discovered the girl, after watching his men get killed, decided that this weird girl was property, with no rights. That would have been reasonable if he knew that such things as replicants existed.

All of that was my reasonable extrapolation from watching the anime and never reading the light novels. But now I have been informed that the light novels never bothered to explain Violet's origins. Maybe the writer didn't care, or maybe the writer didn't want to disappoint the readers with a half-baked backstory. But I'm a little disappointed. If the writer didn't have a cool origin to explain Violet's super-strength and combat skills, she could have been written without them. She could have been an ordinary girl (either with or without amnesia) who got discovered and somehow avoided getting raped before being dumped onto her love interest. Maybe the writer couldn't imagine a good reason why the love interest would keep an ordinary girl around a military camp, but the writer could imagine the love interest keeping a super-powered girl around a military camp. Maybe the writer wanted to throw in some extra combat scenes to prevent the story from getting too twee for a male audience. Maybe the writer just likes the "Superpowered Girlfriend" trope. But damn it, now I have to take Violet Evergarden off my list of "good stories involving replicants," and I don't think I can forgive the writer for that.
